Subsequently, the matter was heard on 22.5.2025 wherein the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that, in its recent order dated 20.04.2025 in Petition No. (h) The proposed amendment, therefore, does not introduce any new cause of action, nor alter the fundamental character of the Petition. It merely seeks to align the existing pleadings and reliefs with the changed regulatory framework and to facilitate comprehensive adjudication of all issues, including Change in Law events arising after the promulgation of the Change in Law Rules, in conformity with the MUML Order. The amendment thus ensures consistency with the legal position and avoids multiplicity of proceedings, and assists this Commission in determining the real issues in controversy. (p) The Respondents, instead of facilitating expeditious adjudication, have adopted a dilatory approach and are objecting even to the captioned Application seeking amendment to the Petition. The captioned Application has been filed _bona fide_ and with the objective of expeditiously resolving the real controversy between the parties, in line with GMR Warora. Such conduct of the Respondents is contrary to the intent and spirit of the Change in Law Rules and directly contributes to the accrual of ‘carrying cost’, thereby increasing the financial burden on the end- _The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy between the parties:_ As per the above, the Commission may allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings, necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy, in such a manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate _at any stage of proceedings_ in a Petition _._ However, the first _proviso_ stipulates that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the commencement of the final hearing of the Petition, unless the Commission is of the opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the 23. On a careful examination of the IA, it clearly appears that the Petitioner has sought the further amendment to the Petition merely to incorporate its claims of Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, along with the consequential reliefs arising therefrom. Pertinently, the Petition already seeks recognition and declaration of various Force Majeure and Change in Law events that affected the construction of the transmission project and permitting the Petitioner to include the Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, would only allow the effective adjudication of the Petitioner’s claims of Change in Law events that affected the transmission project during the construction phase. Additionally, allowing such an amendment would serve the dominant purpose of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings, as the Petitioner would otherwise be required to file a separate Petition to raise such claims, thereby leading to a fresh round of litigation between the parties over Change in Law events. 26. We have carefully considered the objections raised by the Respondents regarding alleged prejudice, abuse of process, and the delay. The Petitioner has primarily argued that the need for the proposed amendment arose only in view of the change in the regulatory position brought about by the MUML Order. The Petitioner has argued that the Commission, by the said Order, has clarified that no recovery of compensation for Change in Law claims shall commence unless (i) there is express consent from all the beneficiaries of the region, or (ii) the claims have been duly approved by the Commission. As a consequence of this, the Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, for which the Petitioner had earlier reserved its right to file a separate Petition under the Change in Law Rules, are now sought to be incorporated for the adjudication of the Commission in this Petition itself. However, we do not agree with the above submission that the need for the present amendment was triggered by the MUML Order. Noticeably, the position clarified in the MUML Order that the Change in Law Rules do not cover a scenario where the parties are not in agreement with each other as to whether the event constitutes a Change in Law event 29. Similarly, the argument of the Respondents that allowing the amendment will prolong litigation and lead to financial prejudice/ cost escalation of unverified claims is also misplaced. Such prejudice, however, is not caused by the amendment, but by the pendency of the main Petition itself, and can be adequately addressed by granting opportunity to the Respondents to file replies, raise objections, or address the merits at the stage of final adjudication. No irreparable prejudice that cannot be compensated or addressed procedurally has been shown. If the present amendment is refused, the Petitioner would then be required to file a fresh Petition in relation to the events occurring on and after 21.10.2021. This would be contrary to the objective of avoiding multiplicity of litigation. Moreover, as already discussed, the proposed amendment neither seeks to change the Petition’s basic nature nor introduces time-barred claims. In our view, the proposed amendment satisfies the legal tests under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, Regulation 38 of the Conduct of Business Regulations, and the well-established principles governing the Amendment of Pleadings as culled out in _Sanjeev Builders (supra)_ .
